pumac-2008-algebra-b-01.title: Evaluate step by step
pumac-2008-algebra-b-01.body:
$2^6=64$, so $4\cdot 64=256$. The denominator is $11-3=8$, so the fraction is $256/8=32$. Hence $x=2+32=34$.

**Answer: 34**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-02.title: Check $\log_4 8$ directly
pumac-2008-algebra-b-02.body:
$4^{3/2}=(2^2)^{3/2}=2^3=8$, so $\log_4 8=\tfrac32$; the rest follows as above.

**Answer: 9**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-03.title: Sum up to each 1
pumac-2008-algebra-b-03.body:
The $k$-th $1$ is preceded by $k-1$ twos, so the $k$-th $1$ is term number $1+2+\dots+k=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}$ and the sum up to it is $k+2\cdot\frac{k(k-1)}2=k^2$.

For $k=44$: term number $\frac{44\cdot45}{2}=990$ and sum $44^2=1936$. The next $1$ is term $1035$ (sum $2025$), so between terms $991$ and $1034$ every term is a $2$ and the sum goes up by $2$ each time: $1936+2j$.

We need $1936+2j=2008$ (the value $2009$ is odd and never occurs there), so $j=36$ and $n=990+36=1026$.

**Answer: 1026**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-03.title: Check
pumac-2008-algebra-b-03.body:
The first $1026$ terms contain $44$ ones and $982$ twos, with sum $44+1964=2008$. Term $1027$ is a $2$, giving $2010$, so $2009$ is skipped and $n=1026$ is the only one.

**Answer: 1026**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-04.title: Substitute $u=3x+1$
pumac-2008-algebra-b-04.body:
The denominator is $(3x+1)^2+1$, so the expression is $\dfrac{u}{u^2+1}$. By AM-GM, $u^2+1\ge 2|u|$, so $\left|\dfrac{u}{u^2+1}\right|\le \dfrac12$, with equality at $u=\pm1$. Hence the maximum is $\tfrac12$ and the minimum is $-\tfrac12$, and the product is $-\tfrac14$.

**Answer: $-\tfrac14$**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-04.title: Discriminant
pumac-2008-algebra-b-04.body:
Put $y=\dfrac{u}{u^2+1}$. Then $yu^2-u+y=0$ has a real solution $u$ iff $1-4y^2\ge0$ (and $u=0$ gives $y=0$), i.e. $|y|\le\frac12$. Both $\pm\frac12$ are attained, so the product is $-\frac14$.

**Answer: $-\tfrac14$**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-05.title: Factor both
pumac-2008-algebra-b-05.body:
Both polynomials are divisible by $c(x)=x^3-3x+1$:
$$x^5+3x^4-4x^3-8x^2+6x-1=(x^3-3x+1)(x^2+3x-1),$$
$$x^5-3x^4-2x^3+10x^2-6x+1=(x^3-3x+1)(x^2-3x+1).$$
The quadratic factors have no common root (subtracting gives $6x-2=0$, $x=\frac13$, which is not a root of $x^2+3x-1$). So the common roots are exactly the roots of $c(x)$.

$c(-2)=-1,\ c(0)=1,\ c(1)=-1,\ c(2)=3$, so by sign changes $c$ has a real root in each of $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$. A cubic has at most three roots, so all three are real.

**Answer: 3**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-06.title: Factor and show $120\mid f(n)$
pumac-2008-algebra-b-06.body:
$f(n)=n(9n^4-5n^2-4)=(n-1)n(n+1)(9n^2+4)$.

- **8:** if $n$ is odd, $8\mid n^2-1=(n-1)(n+1)$; if $n$ is even, $2\mid n$ and $4\mid 9n^2+4$.
- **3:** $(n-1)n(n+1)$ is a product of three consecutive integers.
- **5:** if $n\equiv0,\pm1\pmod5$ then $5\mid (n-1)n(n+1)$; if $n\equiv\pm2$ then $9n^2+4\equiv 36+4=40\equiv0$.

So $120\mid f(n)$ for every integer $n$.

pumac-2008-algebra-b-06.title: Show nothing larger divides all of them
pumac-2008-algebra-b-06.body:
$f(17)=12754080$, $f(18)=16976880$, $f(19)=22250520$, $f(20)=28759920$ and $\gcd\bigl(f(17),f(18),f(19),f(20)\bigr)=120$. Since $120$ divides every $f(n)$ in the list, the gcd of the whole list is exactly $120$.

**Answer: 120**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-07.title: Take $k$-th roots
pumac-2008-algebra-b-07.body:
The system says $\sqrt[k]{k}<x<\sqrt[k]{k+1}$ for each $k\le n$, i.e. $x$ must lie in all the intervals 
$$(1,2),\ (\sqrt2,\sqrt3),\ (\sqrt[3]3,\sqrt[3]4),\ (\sqrt[4]4,\sqrt[4]5),\ (\sqrt[5]5,\sqrt[5]6).$$
Numerically $\sqrt2\approx1.414,\ \sqrt[3]3\approx1.442,\ \sqrt[4]4\approx1.414$ and the upper ends are $2,\ 1.732,\ 1.587,\ 1.495$, so for $n\le4$ the common range is $(1.442,\,1.495)$, nonempty (e.g. $x=1.47$).

For $k=5$ we would need $\sqrt[5]5<x<\sqrt[5]6\approx1.431$, but already $x>\sqrt[3]3$ forces $x>1.442>\sqrt[5]6$ ($3^5=243>216=6^3$). So $n=5$ is impossible.

**Answer: 4**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-09.title: Degree at least 6, and the answer works
pumac-2008-algebra-b-09.body:
The condition on $g-f$ says $f$ is the smallest such polynomial: lowest degree first, and then the smallest coefficients, read from the top.

**Degree.** If $f$ is monic of degree $d$, its $d$-th finite difference is the constant $d!$, and it is a combination of values of $f$, hence divisible by $72$. Since $5!=120$ is not divisible by $72$ but $6!=720=72\cdot10$ is, $d\ge 6$.

**Candidate.** Adding $72$ to a coefficient never destroys divisibility, so every coefficient of the smallest $f$ lies in $\{0,\dots,71\}$, and $f(0)\equiv0$ forces the constant term to be $0$. Because $f(x+72)\equiv f(x)\pmod{72}$, divisibility only needs checking for $x=0,\dots,71$.

Searching the coefficients from the top (all values of the remaining lower coefficients are checked modulo $72$): the $x^5$ coefficient can be $0$; the $x^4$ coefficient cannot be $0$ but can be $1$; then the $x^3$ coefficient can be $0$; then the smallest possible $x^2$ coefficient is $34$ (every smaller value fails); and finally the smallest $x$ coefficient is $36$.

So $f(x)=x^6+x^4+34x^2+36x$. (A direct check of $f(x)\bmod 8$ and $\bmod 9$ for all residues confirms $72\mid f(x)$ for every integer $x$.)

**Answer: $x^6+x^4+34x^2+36x$**

pumac-2008-algebra-b-10.title: Turn the condition into an identity for $p$
pumac-2008-algebra-b-10.body:
Since $\frac1{1-x}\cdot\bigl(1-\frac1{1-x}\bigr)=-\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}$, the condition $q(x)=q\!\left(\frac1{1-x}\right)$ reads
$$\frac{p(x)}{x(1-x)}=-\frac{(1-x)^2}{x}\,p\!\left(\tfrac1{1-x}\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(x)=-(1-x)^3\,p\!\left(\tfrac1{1-x}\right).$$
If $p$ had degree $m>3$, the right side would have a pole of order $m-3$ at $x=1$, so $\deg p\le3$. Write $p=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$. Then $-(1-x)^3p\left(\frac1{1-x}\right)=-\bigl[a+b(1-x)+c(1-x)^2+d(1-x)^3\bigr]$, and comparing coefficients with $p(x)$ gives $a=d$ and $b+c=-3a$.

Now $p(2)=9a+4b+2c=-7$ and $p(3)=28a+9b+3c=-11$. Substituting $c=-3a-b$: $3a+2b=-7$ and $19a+6b=-11$, so $a=1$, $b=-5$, $c=2$, $d=1$:
$$p(x)=x^3-5x^2+2x+1,\qquad p(10)=1000-500+20+1=521.$$

**Answer: 521**
